facts.title: Hidden in the Air
facts.text: Krypton was discovered in 1898 by William Ramsay and Morris Travers in London while studying the residue left after evaporating nearly all of a sample of liquid air. They named it from the Greek word 'kryptos', meaning 'hidden', because it had stayed concealed in the atmosphere. In the same remarkable few weeks the pair also isolated neon and xenon from the same air residues.

facts.title: A Rare Breath of Air
facts.text: Despite being all around us, krypton makes up only about 1.1 parts per million of Earth's atmosphere by volume, roughly one atom in every 900,000. The only practical way to obtain it is by fractional distillation of liquefied air, which is why it remains relatively expensive. The entire atmosphere holds krypton, yet you would inhale only trace amounts with every breath.

facts.title: It Once Defined the Meter
facts.text: From 1960 to 1983 the meter was officially defined using krypton-86: exactly 1,650,763.73 wavelengths of the orange-red light it emits in an electric discharge. This replaced an aging platinum-iridium metal bar as the world standard for length. Krypton lost the honor only when the meter was redefined in terms of the speed of light.

facts.title: Noble, But Not Inert
facts.text: For decades chemists believed the noble gases formed no compounds at all, but krypton proved them slightly wrong. Krypton difluoride (KrF2) can be made by exposing a mixture of krypton and fluorine to electrical discharge or ultraviolet light at very low temperatures. It is a powerful oxidizing and fluorinating agent, so reactive that it slowly attacks the containers it is stored in.

facts.title: Light for Airport Runways
facts.text: Krypton gas glows a bright whitish color when electricity passes through it, making it useful in high-intensity lighting. It is used in some airport runway approach lights and in high-speed photographic flash lamps because it can produce brief, brilliant bursts of light. Mixing krypton with argon also improves the efficiency and lifespan of certain fluorescent and incandescent lamps.

facts.title: The Window Gas
facts.text: Krypton's low thermal conductivity makes it an excellent insulator, so it is pumped into the space between panes of high-performance double- and triple-glazed windows. The dense, sluggish gas slows the flow of heat far better than ordinary air, helping buildings stay warm in winter and cool in summer. Krypton-filled windows are thinner than argon-filled ones for the same insulating effect, saving space and weight.

facts.title: A Powerful Eye Surgery Laser
facts.text: The krypton fluoride excimer laser produces deep ultraviolet light at a wavelength of 248 nanometers. This precise, cool-cutting beam is used in laser eye surgery and in photolithography, the process that etches microscopic circuit patterns onto computer chips. The same excimer technology has been explored for driving experimental nuclear fusion research.

facts.title: A Fingerprint of Nuclear Activity
facts.text: Krypton-85 is a radioactive isotope produced by nuclear fission, and it leaks into the atmosphere from nuclear reactors and fuel-reprocessing plants. Because it is chemically unreactive and easy to detect, scientists monitor atmospheric krypton-85 to help estimate global nuclear activity. Its presence is also used by hydrologists to date underground water that fell as rain within roughly the last 50 years.

facts.title: Forged in Exploding Stars
facts.text: Krypton is created in the cosmos through nucleosynthesis inside stars, including the slow neutron-capture process in aging giant stars and the explosive conditions of supernovae. These stellar furnaces build heavier elements that are later scattered into space and recycled into new stars and planets. The krypton in Earth's air is therefore a genuine sample of ancient stellar chemistry.

facts.title: Harmless to Breathe, But Beware
facts.text: Krypton is chemically non-toxic and plays no role in human biology, passing through the body without taking part in any reactions. However, because it is denser than air and inert, a high concentration can displace oxygen and cause suffocation, a real hazard in poorly ventilated spaces. Under high pressure krypton also becomes mildly narcotic, an effect related to the dangers of nitrogen narcosis faced by deep-sea divers.
